## Projective Map Method and Steiner Conic

::: {#thm-10point1}
## Projective map method
Suppose cross ratios are defined on sets $\mathscr{E}$ and $\mathscr{F}$, and let $f, f': \mathscr{E}\to \mathscr{F}$ be two projective maps. If there exist three points $P_1, P_2, P_3\in E$ such that $f(P_i)=f'(P_i)$ for $i=1,2,3$, then $f=f'$. In fact, given any $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3\in F$, there exists a unique projective map $f:\mathscr{E}\to \mathscr{F}$ satisfying $f(P_i)=Q_i$ for $i=1,2,3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
For every $X\in \mathscr{E}$, since both maps preserve cross ratio,
$$
(f(P_1),f(P_2);f(P_3),f(X))=(f'(P_1),f'(P_2);f'(P_3),f'(X)).
$$
Since $f(P_i)=f'(P_i)$ for $i=1,2,3$, this common value equals $(f(P_1),f(P_2);f(P_3),f'(X))$.

By @thm-6point4, $f(X)=f'(X)$ for all $X\in \mathscr{E}$, giving uniqueness $f=f'$.

For existence, we may assume $\mathscr{E}$ and $\mathscr{F}$ are two lines $\ell_P$ and $\ell_Q$ (as we can compose with projective maps $\mathscr{E}\to \ell_P$ and $\ell_Q\to \mathscr{F}$).

Let $\ell_R=P_1Q_2$, pick a point $T$ on $P_2Q_2$, set $R_3=TP_3\cap \ell_R$, and set $S=P_1Q_1\cap Q_3R_3$.

For any $P\in \ell_P$, set $R=TP\cap \ell_R$ and define $f(P)=Q=SR\cap \ell_Q$; then $f$ satisfies the required conditions.
:::

::: {#thm-10point2}
## Desargues's Theorem
Triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$ are perspective from a point if and only if $BC\cap EF$, $CA\cap FD$, and $AB\cap DE$ are collinear.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$ are perspective from a point $P$, and set $U=BC\cap EF$, $V=CA\cap FD$, and $W=AB\cap DE$.

Fix $A,B,C,E,F,P,U$ and let $D$ vary along $AP$, so $V$ and $W$ vary along $AC$ and $AB$, respectively.

Set $W'=VU\cap AB$. The map $f:AP\to AB$ given by $D\mapsto ED\cap AB=W$ is a projective map, and the map $f':AP\to AB$ given by $D\mapsto FD\cap AC=V\mapsto UV\cap AB=W'$ is also a projective map.

Observe that when $D=A$, we have $V=W=W'=A$; when $D=P$, we have $V=C$ and $W=W'=B$; and when $D=AP\cap EF$, we have $V=EF\cap AC$ and $W=W'=EF\cap AB$.

Thus $f(D)=f'(D)$ at these three points, so @thm-10point1 implies $W=f(D)=f'(D)=W'$ for all $D$; hence $U,V,W$ are collinear.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The line containing the three collinear intersection points in @thm-10point2 is called the **perspectrix** (or **axis of perspectivity**) of the two triangles. Thus @thm-10point2 states that two triangles have a center of perspectivity if and only if they have an axis of perspectivity.
:::

::: {#cor-10point1}
The trilinear polar of a point is the perspectrix of the reference triangle and the cevian triangle of that point.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The **envelope** of a conic section $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of all lines tangent to $\mathcal{C}$, denoted $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$.
:::

::: {#unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
For five lines $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4,\ell$, define
$$
\ell(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)=(\ell_1\cap\ell,\ell_2\cap\ell;\ell_3\cap\ell,\ell_4\cap\ell).
$$
:::

::: {#lem-10point1}
Six lines $m,n,\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4$ are tangent to a common conic section if and only if $m(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)=n(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
If $m,n,\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4\in \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$, let $L_i, M, N$ be the points of tangency of $\ell_i, m, n$ with $\mathcal{C}$, respectively.

By @thm-8point1, $M(L_1,L_2;L_3,L_4)=N(L_1,L_2;L_3,L_4)$.

Since a polar transformation preserves cross ratio, $m(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)=n(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)$.

Conversely, if $m(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)=n(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)$, let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic tangent to $m,n,\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3$; dualizing the argument of @thm-8point2 via a polar transformation shows that $\ell_4$ is also tangent to $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

::: {#unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
For $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4,\ell\in \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$, as $\ell$ varies in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$, the constant value $\ell(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)$ is called the **cross ratio on the envelope**, denoted $(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)_{\mathcal{C}}$.
:::

::: {#lem-10point2}
Suppose $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4\in \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$, and let $\ell$ be a line not in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$. For each $i$, let $\ell_i'$ be the other line in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$ passing through $\ell_i\cap\ell$. Then $(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)_{\mathcal{C}}=(\ell_1',\ell_2';\ell_3',\ell_4')_{\mathcal{C}}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let a line $m$ touch $\mathcal{C}$ at $M$, and let $\ell_i, \ell_i'$ touch $\mathcal{C}$ at $L_i, L_i'$, respectively.

Under polarity, $L_i, L_i'$, and $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(\ell)$ are collinear, so $L_i\mapsto L_i'$ is a projective map by @lem-8point6.

By @thm-8point5, a polar transformation also preserves cross ratio of points and lines, so the chain
$$
\ell_i\mapsto m\cap \ell_i\mapsto ML_i\mapsto L_i\mapsto L_i'\mapsto ML_i'\mapsto m\cap\ell_i'\mapsto \ell_i'
$$
consists of projective maps.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Interchanging points and lines (replacing incidence of a point on a line with a line through a point) and interchanging conic sections and envelopes (replacing a point on a conic with a line tangent to a conic) in a projective geometry statement produces its **dual statement**.
:::

::: {#cor-10point2}
A statement and its dual need only one proof, since replacing point and line cross ratios with their duals leaves the rest of the proof identical.
:::

::: {#lem-10point3}
A polar transformation with respect to a conic $\mathcal{C}$ maps a conic section to the envelope of another conic section and is a projective map. Dually, a polar transformation maps the envelope of a conic section to another conic section and is also a projective map.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $A,B,C,P,Q$ lie on a conic $\mathcal{C}_1$; then there exists a conic $\mathcal{C}_2$ tangent to the polars of these five points with respect to $\mathcal{C}$.

If $X$ also lies on $\mathcal{C}_1$, then $P(A,B;C,X)=Q(A,B;C,X)$. Since a polar transformation preserves cross ratio,
$$
\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(P)(\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(A),\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(B);\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(C),\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(X))
=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(Q)(\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(A),\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(B);\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(C),\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)).
$$
By @lem-10point1, all six polars are tangent to $\mathcal{C}_2$.

The cross ratios above also show that $(A,B;C,X)_{\mathcal{C}_1}=(\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(A),\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(B);\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(C),\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(X))_{\mathcal{C}_2}$, so the map preserves cross ratio.
:::

::: {#thm-10point3}
## Steiner Conic Theorem
Let $\mathbb{L}_P$ and $\mathbb{L}_Q$ be pencils of lines through $P$ and $Q$, respectively, and let $f:\mathbb{L}_P\to \mathbb{L}_Q$ be a projective map. If $f(PQ)=QP$, then the locus of $\ell\cap f(\ell)$ is a line; if $f(PQ)\neq QP$, then the locus of $\ell\cap f(\ell)$ is a conic section passing through $P$ and $Q$ (as $\ell$ varies over $\mathbb{L}_P$).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
If $f(PQ)=QP$, pick $\ell_1,\ell_2\in \mathbb{L}_P\setminus\{PQ\}$, and set $A=\ell_1\cap f(\ell_1)$ and $B=\ell_2\cap f(\ell_2)$.

Since $f$ is a projective map,
$$
(f(\ell_1),f(\ell_2);f(PQ),f(\ell))=(\ell_1,\ell_2;PQ,\ell)=(A,B;PQ\cap AB,\ell\cap AB).
$$
Also,
$$
(f(\ell_1),f(\ell_2);f(PQ),f(\ell))=(A,B;QP\cap AB,f(\ell)\cap AB).
$$
By @thm-6point4, $\ell\cap AB=f(\ell)\cap AB$, so the locus of $\ell\cap f(\ell)$ is the line $AB$.

If $f(PQ)\neq QP$, pick $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3\in \mathbb{L}_P\setminus\{PQ,f^{-1}(QP)\}$, set $A_i=\ell_i\cap f(\ell_i)$, and set $X=\ell\cap f(\ell)$. Then
$$
P(A_1,A_2;A_3,X)=(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell)=(f(\ell_1),f(\ell_2);f(\ell_3),f(\ell))=Q(A_1,A_2;A_3,X).
$$
Since $P,Q,A_1,A_2,A_3$ are not collinear (otherwise cross ratios would force $f(PQ)=QP$, a contradiction), @thm-8point2 implies that $X,P,Q,A_1,A_2,A_3$ lie on a common conic; hence the locus of $\ell\cap f(\ell)$ is a conic through $P$ and $Q$.
:::

::: {#thm-10point4}
Let $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ be two lines, and let $f:\ell_1\to \ell_2$ be a projective map. If $f(\ell_1\cap\ell_2)=\ell_2\cap\ell_1$, then the line $Xf(X)$ passes through a fixed point; if $f(\ell_1\cap\ell_2)\neq \ell_2\cap\ell_1$, then $Xf(X)$ is the envelope of some conic section (as $X$ varies over $\ell_1$).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This is the dual of @thm-10point3.
:::

::: {#cor-10point3}
In @thm-10point3, the map $\ell\mapsto \ell\cap f(\ell)$ is a projective map; in @thm-10point4, the map $X\mapsto Xf(X)$ is also a projective map.
:::

::: {#lem-10point4}
Given a conic section $\mathcal{C}$, $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(BC)\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(CA)\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(AB)$ are perspective.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Set $D=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(BC)$, $E=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(CA)$, and $F=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(AB)$.

Let $\mathcal{C}_1$ be a conic through $A,B,C,D$, and fix $\mathcal{C}$, $\mathcal{C}_1$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ while letting $A$ vary on $\mathcal{C}_1$ (degenerate cases where $A$ lies on a side of $\triangle BCD$ are immediate).

Then $E$ varies along $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(C)$ and $F$ varies along $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(B)$.

By @lem-10point3, $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(A)$ belongs to the envelope of some conic $\mathcal{C}_2$; when $A$ takes the positions $B$ and $C$, $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(A)$ becomes $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(B)$ and $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(C)$, both tangent to $\mathcal{C}_2$.

By @lem-10point3, $A\mapsto \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(A)\mapsto \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(B)\cap \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(A)=F$ is a projective map; similarly $A\mapsto E$ is a projective map, so $f:\mathbb{L}_B\to \mathbb{L}_C$ given by $BE\mapsto E\mapsto A\mapsto F\mapsto CF$ is a projective map.

When $A=D$, $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(A)=BC$, so both $E$ and $F$ lie on $BC$ and $f(BC)=CB$.

By @thm-10point3, the locus of $BE\cap CF$ is a line $\ell$.

Then $g:\mathcal{C}_1\to \ell$ given by $A\mapsto BE\mapsto BE\cap \ell=BE\cap CF$ is a projective map, and $g':\mathcal{C}_1\to \ell$ given by $A\mapsto DA\mapsto DA\cap \ell$ is also a projective map.

Let $B'$ and $C'$ be the second intersections of $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(B)$ and $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(C)$ with $\mathcal{C}_1$, so $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(B)=DB'$ and $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(C)=DC'$.

When $A=B'$, $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(A)$ passes through $B$, so $BE=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(B')$ and $F=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(B')\cap DB'$; thus
$$
g(B')=BE\cap\ell=BE\cap CF=F=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(B')\cap DB'=DB'\cap\ell=g'(B').
$$
Analogously, $g(C')=g'(C')$. When $A=B$, $E=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(A)\cap \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(C)=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(B)\cap \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(C)=D$, so $g(B)=BE\cap\ell=DB\cap\ell=g'(B)$.

By @thm-10point1, $g=g'$; hence $AD$, $BE$, $\ell$, and $CF$ concur, establishing perspectivity.
:::

::: {#lem-10point5}
Let $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$ be a non-identity projective map on a conic $\mathcal{C}$. Then there exists a line $\ell$ such that for all $X,Y\in \mathcal{C}$, the intersection $Xf(Y)\cap Yf(X)$ lies on $\ell$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Given $A, B_1, B_2\in \mathcal{C}$, set $P_i=Af(B_i)\cap f(A)B_i$ ($i=1,2$) and consider the line $\ell=P_1P_2$.

We have
$$
(B_1,B_2;A,X)_{\mathcal{C}}\stackrel{f(A)}{=}(P_1,P_2;Af(A)\cap\ell,Xf(A)\cap\ell),
$$
and also
$$
(B_1,B_2;A,X)_{\mathcal{C}}=(f(B_1),f(B_2);f(A),f(X))_{\mathcal{C}}\stackrel{A}{=}(P_1,P_2;Af(A)\cap\ell,Af(X)\cap\ell).
$$
By @thm-6point4, $Af(X)\cap\ell=Xf(A)\cap\ell$, meaning that for all $X,Y\in\mathcal{C}$, both $Af(X)\cap Xf(A)$ and $Af(Y)\cap Yf(A)$ lie on $\ell$.

By @thm-8point6 on $Af(X)Yf(A)Xf(Y)$, $Xf(Y)\cap Yf(X)$ also lies on $\ell$.
:::

::: {#thm-10point5}
Let $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$ be a projective map on a conic $\mathcal{C}$. Then the line $Xf(X)$ either passes through a fixed point or belongs to the envelope of a conic section; accordingly, the locus of $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(Xf(X))$ is a line or a conic section.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
If $f$ is the identity map, then $Xf(X)$ is tangent to $\mathcal{C}$ and thus belongs to the envelope of $\mathcal{C}$. Assume $f$ is not the identity map.

Given $A\in\mathcal{C}$, let $P=Af(A)\cap Xf(X)$ and $Q=Af(X)\cap Xf(A)$. By @thm-8point3 and @thm-8point4, $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(P)$ passes through both $Q$ and $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(Af(A))$.

By @lem-10point5, let $\ell$ be the line containing $Xf(Y)\cap Yf(X)$ for all $X,Y\in\mathcal{C}$.

If $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(X'f(X'))$ lies on $\ell$ for all $X'\in\mathcal{C}$, then $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(\ell)$ lies on $X'f(X')$ for all $X'\in\mathcal{C}$; since $\ell$ is independent of $X'$, every $X'f(X')$ passes through the fixed point $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(\ell)$.

Otherwise, choose $A\in\mathcal{C}$ such that $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(Af(A))$ does not lie on $\ell$. Then the chain
$$
X\mapsto f(A)X\mapsto \ell\cap f(A)X=Q\mapsto \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(Af(A))Q=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(P)\mapsto P
$$
consists of projective maps.

For fixed $A,B\in\mathcal{C}$ and varying $X\in\mathcal{C}$, write $\ell_A=Af(A)$, $\ell_B=Bf(B)$, and $\ell_X=Xf(X)$. The projective chain above gives
$$
(X_1,X_2;X_3,X)_{\mathcal{C}}=\ell_A(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_X),
$$
and similarly $\ell_A(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_X)=\ell_B(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_X)$.

By @lem-10point1, $\ell_X$ belongs to the envelope of a conic tangent to $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_A,\ell_B$.

Applying a polar transformation with respect to $\mathcal{C}$ (@lem-10point3) shows that the locus of $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}}(Xf(X))$ is a line or a conic section.
:::
